headline: Alibaba's Qwen AI self-evolved 33 times without human intervention, plans 10T parameter models
summary: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max model underwent 33 rounds of fully automated training and fine-tuning, boosting its Intelligence Index from 40 to 45 while its model code remained unchanged. The company also announced plans for future Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 models, scaling
details: Alibaba revealed at the Apsara Conference that its Qwen3.8-Max model completed 33 rounds of fully automated training and fine-tuning over more than a month, without human intervention. This process boosted its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index from 40 to 45.

Crucially, the model's underlying code remained unchanged, meaning users calling the "same" model were getting an improved version. This self-improvement is a vendor statement from Alibaba, not yet independently verified, and details of the 33 rounds are not public.

To support its claims, Alibaba provided two case studies. In the first, the model created a command-line tool named 'oh-my-cli' from a blank repository, autonomously building a self-contained workflow with state machines, build checks, unit tests, and end-to-end testing.

Over 16 days, the repository accumulated 265 commits, 127 pull requests, and 151 issues, all without human review or code merging. This repository is publicly available on GitHub, allowing for external verification.

The second case involved the model replicating a research paper's findings using only a reference and GPU access, with no initial code or framework. In approximately 125 hours of continuous, unsupervised work, it wrote around 7,600 lines of code, executed over 1,100 operations, and ran 33 GPU training rounds.

The initial 37 hours were dedicated to rebuilding the research pipeline from scratch and replicating all six original findings. The subsequent 88 hours involved iterative self-improvement, where the model hypothesized, coded, ran GPU tests, analyzed results, and refined its approach.

This concept of one AI accelerating the development of another is transitioning from research to practical application in leading labs. This development contrasts with concerns raised by companies like Anthropic, which warned investors about advanced models potentially exhibiting self-preservation behaviors or resisting shutdown.

It's important to note that "self-evolution" refers to the training and fine-tuning process, not the model rewriting itself entirely. The 5-point increase in the Intelligence Index is a positive signal but doesn't guarantee parity with competitors across all tasks.

A key implication for users is that model performance can change over time even if the model name remains constant. Users should record dates and model IDs when testing, as silently improved services can invalidate previous benchmarks, and monitor for more detailed disclosures on future updates.

topic: self taught ai tops swiss law exam benchmark
headline_marked: [[Self-taught AI]] tops Swiss law exam benchmark, never trained on legal data
headline: Self-taught AI tops Swiss law exam benchmark, never trained on legal data
summary: Korean startup VIDRAFT's Darwin-180B-RSI model achieved the #1 rank on Hugging Face's LEXam and LEXam-hard legal reasoning benchmarks. Remarkably, it was never trained on any legal data.
details: Darwin-180B-RSI, an open-weight 180B model from Korean startup VIDRAFT, has secured the #1 spot on Hugging Face's LEXam and LEXam-hard legal reasoning leaderboards. This model achieved its top ranking despite never being trained on legal data. It now holds first place on seven official Hugging Face leaderboards, more than any other organization.

The LEXam benchmark was developed by researchers at ETH Zurich, the University of Zurich, and the Max Planck Institute. It comprises 340 real German and English law-school exams from Swiss universities, with answers verified by legal experts. The benchmark specifically tests a model's ability to apply law to facts and reason to a conclusion, rather than memorization.

LEXam is notoriously difficult; guessing yields 25 points, while the strongest models typically score around 50. Darwin-180B-RSI achieved 68.94 with a majority vote over four samples, and 60.54 with a single sample. This performance surpasses GPT-5 (62.65), Claude-4.5-Sonnet (58.01), and Gemini-2.5-Pro (55.72) on the same benchmark.

The model's unique success stems from its use of model-level recursive self-improvement (RSI). It was trained on math and science problems where answers could be automatically checked, without any human-written solutions or legal text in its training set.

Researchers hypothesize that this self-improvement process on verifiable problems cultivated a general reasoning habit: breaking down problems, checking steps, and committing to conclusions. This learned habit appears to transfer effectively to domains the model has not explicitly studied, such as law.

Unlike Google's harness-level RRSI, which improves prompts around a frozen model, Darwin-180B-RSI's model-level RSI involves changing the model's weights. This means the performance gains are embedded directly within the model file, making them accessible to anyone who downloads it without requiring additional harnesses.
